sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Phil's ten questions are graph questions
sections.para: Phil Venables lists ten questions a CISO's tool must answer with evidence. Each needs the whole company connected, and each ends in a decision someone holds. Our risk acceptance work supplies that structure, and a twin of an invented retailer in a vault answers all ten, traced to the board.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Ten graph questions, acceptance, and a twin
sections.para: His questions need a graph; the right connections make answers obvious; risk acceptance gives holders and a chain to the board; a twin answers all ten; vaults, behaviour policies and back-testing fit the workflow.

sections.label: Ten questions a tool should answer
sections.para: Many CISO tools are old platforms with AI added. A large company's CISO needs insight, through a tool that federates specialist context graphs. The ten questions run from budget to blast radius, and he asks for a knowledge graph, measured data and back-testing, not an LLM wrapper.

sections.label: Every question is a graph question
sections.line: No question can be answered from one part
sections.para: Budget, process, supplier, identity and acceptance questions each traverse different parts of the company. With the right connections and the irrelevant nodes removed, the answer becomes obvious. Federation needs edges between specialist worlds, not one shared schema.

sections.label: Half of this already exists: risk acceptance
sections.line: Risk acceptance already has half of it
sections.para: Every risk is carried by someone until a date; the only doors are accept for an interval, fund or fix; every holder has a boss up to the board. Cutting budget, revisiting acceptances and cheaper controls are all acceptance decisions.

sections.label: The twin
sections.line: An invented retailer, answered on one graph
sections.para: Thistlewood has four board risks, sixteen risks, 15 controls, 38 incidents and 100 identities. An extra £250k cuts about a million pounds of expected loss; 29 of 40 agents reach beyond their mandate; warehouse ransomware is the scenario its minimum processes cannot withstand.

sections.label: How our workflow fits
sections.para: Each decision is a vault record; agents' behaviour policies make mandate data to compare with reach; answers rest on measured sources and a back-test exposes model errors; a real company keeps specialist tools connected by edges.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.para: The twin is invented, its model deliberately simple, and it shows what graph answers look like rather than being the tool. The questions are Phil's; the reading is Dinis's.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Phil's essay and the earlier risk work
sections.para: Phil Venables' essay of 19 October 2026, the risk acceptance article and vaults, fractal risk registers, and related newsroom articles.
